transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brought you in today?

Yeah, so… the main thing that kind of pushed me to finally make an appointment is work. I’m a claims processing clerk, and I’m supposed to be at my workstation reviewing claims and policies and just getting through them steadily. But I keep getting up during the day, like leaving my desk when I know I really need to stay there and finish the claim reviews.

It’s not even always for some important reason. Sometimes I’ll just stand up or walk away, and then I’m like, “Why did I do that? I need to be at my station.” It’s been bothering me because I know what I’m supposed to do, and I’m trying to do it, but staying put long enough to get through the work has been harder than it should be. That’s probably the biggest reason I’m here.

When you get up from your desk, do you notice an inner feeling of restlessness or a physical urge to move that makes it hard to sit still, or does it feel more like you just lose track of what you're doing and end up wandering off?

I think it’s more like… I just end up getting away from what I’m supposed to be doing. I wouldn’t describe it as, like, this strong physical urge where my body has to move or I’m crawling out of my skin. It’s more that I’m sitting there with the claims open, and I know I’m supposed to keep reviewing them, and then somehow I’m standing up or walking off from my workstation.

And that’s really the thing that pushed me to come in, because it keeps happening during the day even when I know I need to stay put and finish the claim reviews. I’ll be aware afterward, like, “Okay, I shouldn’t have left my desk, I need to get back to this,” but in the moment it’s like I drift away from the task and then I’m not where I’m supposed to be.
Thinking back, did you notice similar problems with staying focused or sticking to tasks when you were a kid or teenager, or is this something that's really only become an issue more recently?

Yeah, looking back, I don’t think this is totally brand new. I mean, it’s more obvious now because work has such specific expectations, like I’m supposed to sit there and move through claims in a steady way, but when I think back to school, there were definitely signs.

In elementary school especially, I remember teachers writing things like, I was bright or capable, but I’d lose worksheets, or I’d miss instructions, or I’d need reminders to actually finish the classwork. Like I wasn’t trying to be difficult, and I don’t remember thinking I didn’t care. It was more that I’d somehow not have the paper I needed, or I’d realize everyone else had started something and I hadn’t fully caught what we were supposed to do, or the teacher would have to come by and nudge me to finish.

So… yeah, I guess it’s not like it appeared out of nowhere recently. It feels like the same kind of pattern, just now it’s causing bigger problems because I’m not a kid in a classroom anymore.
Do you notice yourself frequently interrupting others, blurting out answers or comments before someone finishes speaking, or having trouble waiting your turn in conversations or lines?

Um… I don’t think that’s really one of the main things I’ve noticed, honestly. Like, I’m trying to think of specific examples, and I’m not sure I’d say I’m constantly interrupting people or blurting things out before they’re done.

I mean, I probably have normal moments where I jump in because I think I know what someone’s saying, or I get excited and say something too soon, but not in a way that people are always calling me out for it or where it feels like a big pattern. And waiting in lines is annoying, sure, but I don’t think I have some major problem with it beyond just being impatient like anyone else sometimes.

So… yeah, compared to the desk and task stuff, that doesn’t really stand out to me as a major issue.
Outside of work, do you notice yourself fidgeting a lot, feeling restless when you're supposed to be relaxing, or talking more than people around you in social situations?

Yeah, I mean… somewhat. I wouldn’t say I’m, like, pacing around the house all night or unable to relax in a dramatic way, but in situations where I’m supposed to sit still for a while, I definitely notice it.

Like in trainings at work, or longer team meetings, I’m usually doing something with my body even if I’m trying to look like I’m paying attention. I’ll be bouncing my leg under the table, or clicking my pen, or shifting around in the chair a lot. Sometimes I’ll catch myself doing it because I realize the pen clicking is probably annoying, and then I stop, but then I’m moving my foot or adjusting how I’m sitting instead.

It’s not that I’m trying to be disruptive or anything. It’s more like sitting there completely still feels hard to maintain, especially when the meeting goes on for a while. Socially, I don’t know that I talk way more than everyone else, but the fidgeting in meetings or trainings is definitely something I do.

Going back to when you were a kid, do you remember having that same kind of restlessness or fidgeting—like needing to move, tap, or shift around when you were supposed to sit still in class—or does that feel like something that's newer for you?

I’m not totally sure how far back it goes, honestly. Like, I can remember the school focus stuff more clearly than the physical restlessness stuff. I don’t have a super vivid memory of, you know, being the kid who was always getting in trouble for getting out of his seat or anything like that.

But the fidgeting part… I mean, it feels familiar, if that makes sense. Like even now, in trainings or longer team meetings, I’m usually bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, shifting around in the chair, doing something with my hands or feet, even when I’m trying to look focused and not draw attention to myself. It’s not like I’m trying to be annoying, it’s just hard to sit there completely still for that long.

As a kid, I can’t say for sure if it was exactly the same or how much teachers noticed it. I wouldn’t want to overstate it. But the feeling of needing to move around a little when I’m supposed to sit still doesn’t feel totally new to me either. It’s just that I remember it more clearly now in work settings, because I’m aware of trying to look professional and not distract people.
{"intent": "Determine whether inattentive symptoms (e.g., losing track of tasks, forgetfulness

Yeah… that one definitely happens. Probably more than I like admitting, honestly.

At work especially, it’ll be these small follow-up things that I fully intend to do, and then they just slip out of my head. Like I’ll mean to call a claimant back after I finish looking at something, or I’ll need to update a diary note, or send out a form that I already mentally told myself, “Okay, I’ll send that before the end of the day.” And then later I’ll realize I never did it.

It’s frustrating because it’s usually not that I don’t care or I’m blowing it off on purpose. In the moment, I really do think I’m going to remember. I’ll be like, “I just have to finish this other thing first,” and then I get pulled into the next claim or another email or whatever, and by the time I come back around, the original follow-up is just gone from my mind until something reminds me.

So, yeah, simple things like returning calls, updating notes, sending forms — those are the kinds of things I forget more often than I’m comfortable with.

Do you find it hard to engage in quiet leisure activities—like reading or watching a show—without feeling restless or needing to get up, or do you often feel like you're 'on the go' even during downtime?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that one. I don’t think I feel like I’m constantly “on the go” during downtime, at least not in a really obvious way.

Like, if I’m watching a show, I can usually sit through it, especially if I’m actually interested in it. I might change positions or look at my phone or get up to grab water or something, but I don’t know that I’d describe it as this strong inner restlessness where I can’t relax at all. Reading is harder for me sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s because I feel physically restless versus just not staying with it mentally.

So… I guess I’d say I haven’t really noticed that as a major thing outside of situations where I’m expected to sit still for a long time, like meetings or trainings. Downtime doesn’t usually feel like I have to be moving nonstop.
Do people ever comment that you talk more than others in conversations or meetings, or that you have trouble stopping once you start talking?

I don’t think so, not in a way that people have pointed out to me. I mean, I can definitely ramble sometimes if I’m talking about something I’m really interested in or if I’m trying to explain the whole background of something, because I don’t always know what details are important and what aren’t. Like even now I’m probably giving more explanation than you asked for.

But as far as people actually saying, “You talk too much,” or “You won’t stop talking,” I can’t really think of that being a common complaint. In meetings at work, I’m usually more on the careful side because I don’t want to say something wrong or waste people’s time. If anything, I might over-explain when I do speak up, especially if I’m nervous or trying to make sure I’m understood, but I don’t think I’m usually dominating the conversation.

So… no, I wouldn’t say that’s a big thing people comment on.
Outside of work, do you notice similar problems—like forgetting tasks, losing things, or feeling disorganized—affecting things like your home life, finances, or relationships?

Yeah, I mean… the clearest example that comes to mind is still work, honestly. That’s where it shows up the most because there are so many little follow-up tasks that all kind of stack on top of each other.

Like I’ll fully mean to return a claimant’s call, or I’ll look at a file and think, “Okay, I need to update that diary note,” or I’ll remember there’s a form I need to send out before the end of the day. And it’s not like I’m deciding not to do it — I really do intend to. But then I’ll move on to the next thing, or an email comes in, or I’m checking another claim, and somehow that original task just falls out of my head.

Then later I’ll see the file again or someone follows up, and I get that awful feeling of, “Oh, right, I never did that.” It’s usually simple stuff too, which makes it more frustrating, because it feels like it should be easy to just remember. But I forget those little follow-ups more than I want to admit.

Have people close to you—like a partner, roommate, or family member—ever complained about your forgetfulness, disorganization, or restlessness affecting things at home, such as missing bills, chores, or appointments?

Yeah… I mean, people close to me have noticed the forgetfulness more than the restlessness, I think. I’m trying to think of home examples, but honestly the thing that stands out the most is still the work follow-up stuff.

Like I’ll mean to return a claimant’s call, or I’ll see that I need to update a diary note, or there’s a form I’m supposed to send out earlier in the day, and I genuinely intend to do it. It’s not like I’m blowing it off. But then I get pulled into something else, or I move on to another file, and it just kind of disappears from my mind until later.

And then when it comes back up, I feel embarrassed because it’s usually something simple. It’s not some complicated task. It’s just, “Call this person back,” or “send that form,” and somehow I still miss it. So if people are frustrated with me, it’s usually that kind of thing — me forgetting something I said I was going to do, more than being restless or anything like that.

target_item.name: Fidgeting
target_item.manifestation: In trainings or longer team meetings, I’m usually bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, or shifting around in the chair even when I’m trying to look focused.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hyperactive behaviors outside work, especially fidgeting; this matches the profile item about frequent fidgeting.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean… somewhat. I wouldn’t say I’m, like, pacing around the house all night or unable to relax in a dramatic way, but in situations where I’m supposed to sit still for a while, I definitely notice it.

Like in trainings at work, or longer team meetings, I’m usually doing something with my body even if I’m trying to look like I’m paying attention. I’ll be bouncing my leg under the table, or clicking my pen, or shifting around in the chair a lot. Sometimes I’ll catch myself doing it because I realize the pen clicking is probably annoying, and then I stop, but then I’m moving my foot or adjusting how I’m sitting instead.

It’s not that I’m trying to be disruptive or anything. It’s more like sitting there completely still feels hard to maintain, especially when the meeting goes on for a while. Socially, I don’t know that I talk way more than everyone else, but the fidgeting in meetings or trainings is definitely something I do.

inference.note: Childhood-onset inattentive symptoms confirmed with cross-situational impairment (school, work, meetings); hyperactive-impulsive symptoms present but mild/subthreshold (fidgeting, restlessness) without significant interrupting/blurting. Still consistent with combined or predominantly inattentive presentation, so both codes remain until further symptom count clarification.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the hyperactive/restless symptoms (fidgeting, difficulty staying still) have been present since childhood or are a more recent development, to clarify if this reflects a stable early-onset pattern supporting a specific ADHD presentation versus an unclear/inconsistent history.
doctor.question: Going back to when you were a kid, do you remember having that same kind of restlessness or fidgeting—like needing to move, tap, or shift around when you were supposed to sit still in class—or does that feel like something that's newer for you?

target_item.name: Fidgeting
target_item.manifestation: In trainings or longer team meetings, I’m usually bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, or shifting around in the chair even when I’m trying to look focused.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about restlessness or fidgeting, such as needing to move, tap, or shift around when expected to sit still.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how far back it goes, honestly. Like, I can remember the school focus stuff more clearly than the physical restlessness stuff. I don’t have a super vivid memory of, you know, being the kid who was always getting in trouble for getting out of his seat or anything like that.

But the fidgeting part… I mean, it feels familiar, if that makes sense. Like even now, in trainings or longer team meetings, I’m usually bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, shifting around in the chair, doing something with my hands or feet, even when I’m trying to look focused and not draw attention to myself. It’s not like I’m trying to be annoying, it’s just hard to sit there completely still for that long.

As a kid, I can’t say for sure if it was exactly the same or how much teachers noticed it. I wouldn’t want to overstate it. But the feeling of needing to move around a little when I’m supposed to sit still doesn’t feel totally new to me either. It’s just that I remember it more clearly now in work settings, because I’m aware of trying to look professional and not distract people.

inference.note: Continued evidence of inattentive symptoms since childhood plus mild hyperactive-impulsive traits (fidgeting, restlessness in meetings) without significant interrupting/impulsivity. This supports combined presentation but childhood hyperactivity is unclear, so both predominantly inattentive and unspecified ADHD remain candidates pending further clarification of hyperactive-impulsive symptom count/history.

doctor.question: {"intent": "Determine whether inattentive symptoms (e.g., losing track of tasks, forgetfulness

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: I forget simple work follow-ups more than I want to admit, like returning a claimant’s call, updating a diary note, or sending a form I meant to send earlier that day.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is asking about inattentive symptoms involving forgetfulness or losing track of tasks, which is most directly covered by forgetting work follow-ups like calls, notes, or forms.

patient.answer:
Yeah… that one definitely happens. Probably more than I like admitting, honestly.

At work especially, it’ll be these small follow-up things that I fully intend to do, and then they just slip out of my head. Like I’ll mean to call a claimant back after I finish looking at something, or I’ll need to update a diary note, or send out a form that I already mentally told myself, “Okay, I’ll send that before the end of the day.” And then later I’ll realize I never did it.

It’s frustrating because it’s usually not that I don’t care or I’m blowing it off on purpose. In the moment, I really do think I’m going to remember. I’ll be like, “I just have to finish this other thing first,” and then I get pulled into the next claim or another email or whatever, and by the time I come back around, the original follow-up is just gone from my mind until something reminds me.

So, yeah, simple things like returning calls, updating notes, sending forms — those are the kinds of things I forget more often than I’m comfortable with.

inference.note: Continued evidence of inattentive symptoms (forgetfulness, losing track of tasks, distractibility) since childhood, plus some hyperactive-impulsive features (fidgeting, restlessness in meetings), but not significant interruptting/blurting behavior. This supports a combined presentation, keeping both F90.0 (predominantly inattentive-type may not fit since some hyperactive symptoms exist) and F90.9 (unspecified ADHD) as candidates until further clarification on severity/impact across settings.

doctor.intent: Assess whether hyperactive-impulsive symptoms extend beyond fidgeting to other domains (e.g., difficulty engaging quietly in leisure activities, feeling 'on the go', or excessive talking) to determine if enough symptoms are present for a combined presentation versus an unspecified/inattentive-predominant picture
doctor.question: Do you find it hard to engage in quiet leisure activities—like reading or watching a show—without feeling restless or needing to get up, or do you often feel like you're 'on the go' even during downtime?

target_item.reason: The question is about restlessness during quiet leisure activities or feeling 'on the go' during downtime, which is not specifically covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to answer that one. I don’t think I feel like I’m constantly “on the go” during downtime, at least not in a really obvious way.

Like, if I’m watching a show, I can usually sit through it, especially if I’m actually interested in it. I might change positions or look at my phone or get up to grab water or something, but I don’t know that I’d describe it as this strong inner restlessness where I can’t relax at all. Reading is harder for me sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s because I feel physically restless versus just not staying with it mentally.

So… I guess I’d say I haven’t really noticed that as a major thing outside of situations where I’m expected to sit still for a long time, like meetings or trainings. Downtime doesn’t usually feel like I have to be moving nonstop.

inference.note: Continued endorsement of inattentive symptoms (forgetfulness, task follow-through) and mild hyperactive-impulsive traits (fidgeting in meetings) with childhood onset supports ADHD combined presentation; no new disorders ruled in or out this turn.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient talks excessively or more than others in social/work situations, a key hyperactive-impulsive symptom needed to determine if the combined type threshold is met
doctor.question: Do people ever comment that you talk more than others in conversations or meetings, or that you have trouble stopping once you start talking?

target_item.reason: The question asks about excessive talking or difficulty stopping once talking, which is not covered by any listed symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, not in a way that people have pointed out to me. I mean, I can definitely ramble sometimes if I’m talking about something I’m really interested in or if I’m trying to explain the whole background of something, because I don’t always know what details are important and what aren’t. Like even now I’m probably giving more explanation than you asked for.

But as far as people actually saying, “You talk too much,” or “You won’t stop talking,” I can’t really think of that being a common complaint. In meetings at work, I’m usually more on the careful side because I don’t want to say something wrong or waste people’s time. If anything, I might over-explain when I do speak up, especially if I’m nervous or trying to make sure I’m understood, but I don’t think I’m usually dominating the conversation.

So… no, I wouldn’t say that’s a big thing people comment on.

inference.note: Inattentive symptoms (task drift, forgetfulness, childhood history) remain prominent; hyperactive symptoms are present but subtler (fidgeting in meetings) with hyperactive-impulsive criteria (interrupting, talkativeness, inner restlessness) largely not met. This supports combined presentation but not yet definitively confirmed over unspecified ADHD; continuing to narrow toward F90.0 given cross-setting, childhood-onset inattentive and mild hyperactive symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean… the clearest example that comes to mind is still work, honestly. That’s where it shows up the most because there are so many little follow-up tasks that all kind of stack on top of each other.

Like I’ll fully mean to return a claimant’s call, or I’ll look at a file and think, “Okay, I need to update that diary note,” or I’ll remember there’s a form I need to send out before the end of the day. And it’s not like I’m deciding not to do it — I really do intend to. But then I’ll move on to the next thing, or an email comes in, or I’m checking another claim, and somehow that original task just falls out of my head.

Then later I’ll see the file again or someone follows up, and I get that awful feeling of, “Oh, right, I never did that.” It’s usually simple stuff too, which makes it more frustrating, because it feels like it should be easy to just remember. But I forget those little follow-ups more than I want to admit.

doctor.question: Have people close to you—like a partner, roommate, or family member—ever complained about your forgetfulness, disorganization, or restlessness affecting things at home, such as missing bills, chores, or appointments?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about forgetfulness affecting home responsibilities like bills, chores, or appointments, which most directly matches daily activities forgetfulness.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, people close to me have noticed the forgetfulness more than the restlessness, I think. I’m trying to think of home examples, but honestly the thing that stands out the most is still the work follow-up stuff.

Like I’ll mean to return a claimant’s call, or I’ll see that I need to update a diary note, or there’s a form I’m supposed to send out earlier in the day, and I genuinely intend to do it. It’s not like I’m blowing it off. But then I get pulled into something else, or I move on to another file, and it just kind of disappears from my mind until later.

And then when it comes back up, I feel embarrassed because it’s usually something simple. It’s not some complicated task. It’s just, “Call this person back,” or “send that form,” and somehow I still miss it. So if people are frustrated with me, it’s usually that kind of thing — me forgetting something I said I was going to do, more than being restless or anything like that.

inference.note: Patient endorses persistent inattentive symptoms (forgetfulness, losing track of tasks, distractibility) with childhood onset, plus some hyperactive-impulsive features (fidgeting, difficulty sitting still in meetings) though fewer than full threshold for hyperactive presentation alone. Hyperactive/impulsive symptoms like interrupting, excessive talking, and inability to engage in quiet leisure are largely absent, ruling out predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation, but combined presentation (F90.2) remains less likely given inattentive symptoms clearly predominate. Narrowing to combined presentation code F90.0 as ICD-10 does not further subtype by presentation the way DSM-5 does, and F90.9 (unspecified) is no longer needed given clear symptom pattern consistent with hyperkinetic disorder criteria.
